#1762. The Rock of London: Looking back at John Terry’s Chelsea FC career

Home » Home 2 » The Rock of London: Looking back at John Terry’s Chelsea FC career

At the start of this season, John Terry leaving Chelsea was the last thing on anyone’s mind. All was rosy at Stamford Bridge, the home of the newly crowed English champions. In over 21 years at the club, there was no indication that Terry would not retire a Chelsea man.

The Blues’ skipper’s announcement in January 2016, then, came as a shock to the Chelsea faithful, bringing notice to the seemingly premature — even if inevitable — fall of the curtain on a legendary career.

After making his debut in the League Cup against Aston Villa late in 1998, John Terry made sporadic appearances under Gianluca Vialli, before joining Nottingham Forest on a short loan spell. He broke into the first team in 2000-01, when manager Claudio Ranieri handed him 22 Premier League appearances during a season that the 20-year-old would finish as the club’s Player of the Year.

It would be the first of several achievements to come.

Terry’s importance to the team grew as Ranieri relied on his partnership with then-captain Marcel Desailly to mastermind Chelsea’s progression from a fashionable mid-table club to a Champions League team that meant business. They received a major shot in the arm when Russian billionaire Roman Abramovich bought the club in 2003. It was also a significant year in Terry’s international career as he made his England debut against Serbia and Montenegro in June.

The season that followed saw Chelsea finish above perennial winners Manchester United for the first time in Premier League history, and defeat Premiership invincibles Arsenal en route to the club’s first Champions League semifinal. Terry ended the season making a first of four appearances in the PFA Team of the Year, and went to Portugal for the European Championships having displaced Sol Campbell as England’s first choice centre-back.

In the summer of 2004, Chelsea brought in Jose Mourinho, who was fresh from winning a treble with the unfancied FC Porto and raring to take on bigger challenges. The 23-year-old Terry was named captain as Chelsea embarked on the most successful period in the club’s history. In the three seasons that followed, Chelsea won 2 league cups, 2 Premier League titles and the FA Cup — success built on a core of John Terry, Frank Lampard, Petr Cech and Didier Drogba, Chelsea’s ‘old guard’.

This was also a period when Terry picked up several individual accolades. He was named PFA Player of the Year in 2005, the first defender to win the award since Paul McGrath in 1993. He would make a first of five consecutive appearances in the FIFPro World XI in 2005, as well as a first of four appearances in the UEFA Team of the Year.

He was also voted Chelsea’s Player of the Year for the second time in his career in 2006. Steve McClaren, hired as England manager after an underwhelming 2006 World Cup, named the Chelsea skipper as England captain.

Terry was now, beyond argument, one of football’s best.

However, more testing times were to come.

September 2007 saw the departure of Mourinho after a falling out with the club board. The season itself promised much but left a Chelsea squad dejected on three occasions as they saw the League Cup, the Premier League and the Champions League trophies go elsewhere.

For the European Cup in particular, Terry was left with no one but himself to blame as he slipped for the crucial penalty, a moment he has said will haunt him forever. Chelsea and Terry experienced further European heartbreak the following season as Tom Henning Ovrebo had a refereeing performance to forget at Stamford Bridge, handing Barcelona a berth in the final and eventually the trophy.

In early 2010, when he was revealed as the English footballer who had an affair with Vanessa Perroncel, Wayne Bridge’s ex-girlfriend — a horrendous personal error that cost him his status as England captain — it made him the perennial recipient of passionate booing across English grounds. After the revelation, Chelsea travelled to Burnley. Amidst a frosty reception, he scored a late winner to put Carlo Ancelotti’s side back on track in the title race, one they would go on to win in some style. All of this typified John Terry — imperfect, but unshakeable.

Terry had built an unflappable reputation as a top class defender, leader and hard man. He said about himself, “I still say if the ball is there to be won I will go for it, whether with my head or whatever, and if it means us scoring or stopping a goal, I won’t think twice.”

The period that followed, however, was not good for Chelsea or their captain. The team finished the 2010-11 season trophyless, and Carlo Ancelotti paid for it with his job. This was the first of two times in Terry’s career where he and his club would have an extremely underwhelming season following a dominant one, and it also marked the first attempt to phase him out of the first team.

New manager Andre Villas-Boas attempted to introduce a high defensive line that left Terry exposed on a number of occasions, and saw the young Portuguese manager fall back on quicker defenders to implement his system. He was also determined to make lesser use of Frank Lampard and displace Didier Drogba with Fernando Torres. These were unpopular moves that led to poor results and eventually his sacking. Terry was not helped by another personal abberation, mouthing racial profanity at Anton Ferdinand of QPR, an act that saw him land a lengthy ban and damage his position in the England squad almost beyond repair.

Interim manager Roberto Di Matteo reinstated the old guard, and was rewarded with the ultimate prize — the first Champions League in Chelsea’s history.

Terry retired from international football following EURO 2012, leaving him to focus on his club career. However, further rotation was to follow during the reign of Rafael Benitez, who played Terry only in games of lesser importance. This was something he could do with relative impunity owing to the fact that his stock could not have fallen any further among Chelsea fans.

The writing was seemingly on the wall, however. Unsavoury incidents were fresher in the memory than individual accolades, the skipper was out of favour for two seasons running, and was well over 30 years of age. Was John Terry done?

Mourinho did not share the views of Benitez and Villas-Boas. Where they saw a slowing, easily-exposed has-been, he saw an experienced warrior with an excellent reading of the game who could form a title-winning partnership with the quicker Gary Cahill.

Terry grabbed the opportunity he was handed with gusto, performing with excellence in Mourinho’s lower defensive block. The English pair formed the core of a defence that would go on to win the club’s fourth Premier League title in 2015, leading the table from the opening day to the end. It was a landmark achievement for Terry in particular as he played every minute of a league campaign for the first time in his career, aged 34.

Once again they tried to put him down. Once again he fed off it and rose tall.

Chelsea did not start the defence of their title well at all, gathering just 4 points from the first 4 matches. Mourinho, who asked Terry to take the club on his shoulders in 2004 and stood by him for two seasons in his second stint, hauled off his skipper at half-time at the Etihad in the second game of the season, and began to rotate him out of the team, giving an increasing number of starts to the young Kurt Zouma.

The season did not take much of a turn for the better even under interim manager Guus Hiddink, particularly in a defensive sense as the Blues continued to let in goals during a meek climb to the top half of the table, with or without Terry in the side.

A sending off at the Stadium of Light following an injury layoff is not the kind of ending that the fans desired for their beloved captain, who has emerged from the dugout 703 times in Chelsea colours and has been the face of the club through the most successful period in their history.

Offered a new deal by the club last week, the skipper responded, “The contract extension the club has offered me is a different role and I hope everyone will understand I want to take the time to consider it carefully before making a decision.” While fans will hope — for reasons emotional as well as those to do with football — that Terry stays on, the chances look slim.

Should the captain leave the ship, the Blues supporters’ emotions are best summed up by a certain banner that embellishes the Shed End: Captain, Leader, Legend.

#1761. Tragic footballer Jesus de Miguel's devastated club Tenerife vow to financially support his one-year-old daughter until she turns 18 - as fundraiser passes £125,000

Published: 03:12 EST, 8 November 2026 | Updated: 03:12 EST, 8 November 2026

Tenerife have committed to financially supporting the one-year-old baby daughter of Jesus de Miguel following the 30-year-old's tragic death this week.

De Miguel, 30, lost his life following a horror collision with FC Andorra goalkeeper Jesus Owono in the latter stages of a second division game on the Spanish island.

The striker's girlfriend, Maria Fernandez, and their daughter, Carla, witnessed the incident from the stands. A post-mortem found De Miguel died from 'accidental chest trauma'. It is described in the preliminary report as a 'cause consistent with the player's death'.

The footballing world came together in Tenerife on Thursday for the 30-year-old's funeral, with De Miguel's team-mates, Spain national team coach Luis de la Fuente and Real Madrid president Florentino Perez offering support to his devastated family – who said his passing has left an 'impossible void to fill'.

And now Tenerife have confirmed they will support De Miguel's family and Carla following their loss.

Club CEO Antonio Manuel Porro Granados told The Athletic: 'Our plan is to stand by the girl and make sure the entire Tenerife family supports her. We want to be there for her at least until she reaches adulthood.

Tenerife have vowed to support Jesus De Miguel's one-year-old daughter following his death

Tenerife striker Jesus de Miguel was struck by Jesus Owono during a second division contest and lost his life

'This is a commitment we have made at the initiative of our majority shareholder, Rayco Garcia, and one that we all fully support. It is a commitment that Tenerife, as a club, is making to the family and to their daughter, Carla.

'We will provide the maximum possible support in every respect, beyond what we are legally obliged to provide. We are also exploring other ways of increasing the financial support, so that, at least in material terms, the circumstances do not affect their lives quite so much — although, of course, it is impossible for them not to have an impact.'

Tenerife's commitment follows the development that a fundraiser for the family has passed £125,000 in donations. Spanish footballers Alvaro Morata and Alex Baena are among those who have pledged to the crowdfunding campaign.

De Miguel's family are also reportedly set to receive around £300,000 in base compensation following his death.

Goalkeeper Owono has shut down his Instagram account and retreated from public view amid the significant backlash he has received – which saw him subjected to chants of 'murderer' by the Tenerife fans as he left the pitch.

On Wednesday, he issued a statement describing his 'enormous pain' following the tragic on-field collision.

Owono said: 'These are being the most difficult days of my life. I am struggling to find the words and find it very difficult to assimilate anything that has happened.

Tenerife say they will financially support the family, while a fundraiser has amassed more than £125,000 in donations

'I feel an enormous pain for the loss of Jesús. I think of him, his family, and everyone who loved him. I know there will be many issues to address; I will face whatever comes with the utmost respect.

'But right now, honestly, I cannot think of anything else except Jesús and the pain we are experiencing. Rest in peace, Jesús.'

Police investigating De Miguel's death are probing the emergency medical response as well as the possibility rival goalie Jesus Owono's horror tackle could be involuntary manslaughter.

It emerged on Tuesday that homicide squad officers based in the Tenerife capital Santa Cruz had launched a probe as court officials explained any death 'not resulting from natural causes' automatically triggers a judicial investigation.

Legal experts have said they don't expect the ongoing investigation to lead to criminal charges against Andorra FC goalkeeper Owono because the clash occurred during open play, although he is expected to be hit with a lengthy ban.

#1759. Thibaut Courtois reveals how Jose Mourinho has changed since Chelsea

By Naim Beneddra | 11 Nov 2026 16:14

Real Madrid goalkeeper Thibaut Courtois has revealed that Jose Mourinho is a calmer and less intense manager than the one he worked under at Chelsea 12 years ago, although the Portuguese coach has lost none of his commanding personality.

The Belgium international, who won the Premier League under Mourinho at Stamford Bridge in 2014-15, has been reunited with his former manager following the latter's return to the Santiago Bernabeu during the summer.

Their second spell together has allowed Courtois to observe how Mourinho's approach to managing players has evolved, particularly in the dressing room.

Speaking to Sky Sports during the Web Summit in Lisbon, the 34-year-old suggested that experience has made the former Chelsea boss more measured in his dealings with players.

However, Courtois believes Mourinho's authority remains unmistakable and even suggested that his arrival provided precisely the kind of presence Real Madrid needed.

The goalkeeper also shared an unusual story about their reunion, revealing that he accidentally ignored Mourinho's first message for two weeks while representing Belgium at the 2026 World Cup.

“I think sometimes he’s a bit more calmer” Thibaut Courtois on Jose Mourinho's managerial style at Real Madrid compared to how he was at Chelsea ⏪ https://t.co/9HGnNSTzE2

Courtois was part of the Chelsea squad that secured the Premier League title during Mourinho's second spell in west London, having returned from his loan spell at Atletico Madrid in the summer of 2014.

The pair worked together during a successful 2014-15 campaign, when Chelsea also won the League Cup, before Mourinho left the club in December 2015.

More than a decade later, Courtois believes the Portuguese coach has developed a slightly different approach to handling the demands of an elite dressing room.

"I think he himself says he has maybe grown to be more mature," Courtois explained.

"And with the experience, I think sometimes he is a bit calmer.

"At Chelsea, I remember he was a bit stronger in the dressing room, a bit more intense. Also now he is, but I feel he is a tiny bit less from what I remember from 12 years ago."

The Belgian nevertheless stressed that Mourinho continues to command the attention of everyone around him.

"But he's still the same personality, the same presence," he added.

"He fills the room. When you come in and he's there, you feel he's there. I think that is something that we needed."

Those comments offer an insight into how Mourinho has been received by one of Madrid's most experienced players following his return to the Spanish capital.

The 63-year-old began his second spell at the Bernabeu after Madrid endured a trophyless 2025-26 campaign, with Courtois among the senior figures already familiar with his methods.

Mourinho's side have recovered from two early La Liga defeats to establish an eight-match winning streak across all competitions.

That sequence includes a 2-1 victory over Barcelona at Camp Nou on October 25 and last weekend's 3-0 success against Valencia.

Madrid have also won their opening four Champions League matches, leaving them well placed to secure direct qualification for the knockout stages.

In La Liga, they sit three points behind leaders Barcelona after 12 matches, having accumulated 30 points from 10 victories.

Despite his enthusiasm about working with Mourinho again, Courtois admitted their reunion began with a communication mishap.

The goalkeeper was away with Belgium at the World Cup when Mourinho first attempted to contact him following his appointment at Real Madrid.

However, the message arrived while Courtois was travelling, and he failed to notice it amid the disruption caused by the flight and the time difference.

"He texted me when he arrived in Madrid, but I ignored his message for two weeks," Courtois revealed.

"We were at the World Cup at the time, and the day he texted me, we were on a plane."

The Belgian explained that the lack of Wi-Fi meant several messages went unnoticed, with the misunderstanding only becoming clear when Mourinho contacted him again after an international match.

"Later, after a match, he texted me again, and I asked someone at Real Madrid, 'Is this the coach's number?' But everything is fine now."

The incident did nothing to diminish Courtois's enthusiasm about their reunion.

The goalkeeper explained that he and Mourinho had parted on good terms when the manager left Chelsea and that he had been looking forward to working under him again.

For Courtois, the most significant change is not in Mourinho's authority but in how he exercises it.

That assessment comes at an encouraging moment for Madrid, who will attempt to extend their winning sequence when they host Celta Vigo on November 21 following the international break.

The reunion has already produced positive results, and Courtois's account suggests that Mourinho has found a balance between the demanding management style that defined his Chelsea years and a more measured approach at the Bernabeu.

#1758. Liverpool 0-1 Arsenal: Resolute Gunners dig in for a big Anfield win

Fourteen years is a long time to wait for a win at any stadium, but Arsenal ensured all three points returned from Anfield to North London for the first time since 2012 yesterday.

The surprise in the team line-up was the return of Christos Tzolis who had missed a month, more or less, with a hamstring injury. If it initially felt a bit harsh on Eberechi Eze, Mikel Arteta’s post-game comments about him barely making the game because of an injury problem of his own made it make more sense.

Early on, we were really good. Plenty of the ball, playing it well in their half, and lots of control. Liverpool looked a bit off the pace, and in the opening minutes young midfielder Trey Nyoni was lucky to escape without some sanction for a nasty foul on Martin Odegaard. I think it was much more mistimed than malicious, but studs down the Achilles is never good, and we saw Crystal Palace striker Jean Philippe Mateta see red for something similar on Saturday evening.

The early pressure paid dividends when Liverpool were a little sloppy at the back. Odegaard pounced to recover the ball, it was fed to Noni Madueke via Bruno Guimaraes, and when Declan Rice overlapped, his precision ball to the back post found Kai Havertz for a tap-in to make it 1-0. That makes it 5 assists so far this season for the midfielder, all of them from open play as well, and his presence in this team reminds me so much of Patrick Vieira. Not that they’re the same kind of player, but that his importance and stature is just fundamental to us. The desire he showed with that overlap is, essentially, what cracked this game open in our favour.

There was another back post chance for Havertz, almost getting on the end of a deflected Guimaraes shot, but after that – as happens so often at Anfield – the momentum changed. This time there was no Granit Xhaka style confrontation to act as a catalyst, the game just shifted and in the final 20 minutes of the first half we rode our luck a bit.

Liverpool started to play around our box and deliver dangerous balls. One almost found Alexander Isak but a combination of David Raya and Ezri Konsa was enough to see it trickle wide. Florian Wirtz hit the bar with a free kick, and Liverpool wanted a penalty when Tzolis looked to pull back Cody Gakpo but I don’t think there was enough in that one. The next one, however, oooof.

Liverpool put in another dangerous cross, Isak was there to head towards goal from close range, and Jurrien Timber’s shirt pull absolutely prevented him from making contact with the ball. You know my rule of thumb with penalties: how would I feel it were given, or not given, up the other end, and if we didn’t get that I’d be fuming. It’s a penalty all day long, and even if the ref didn’t quite see the foul well enough, the VAR officials really ought to have suggested an on-field review. I found the focus on Isak’s reaction a bit odd. Surely the onus is on the officials to recognise what we’ve all seen without a player having to prompt them in that direction, but we got so, so lucky there.

As we did when Alexis Mac Allister ran into the box and, unmarked from 10 yards out, headed the ball over the bar when he absolutely should score. That was a very bad miss from a Liverpool perspective, and a huge chance to equalise just before the break. We needed half-time, and despite the fact Liverpool enjoyed plenty of the ball in the early part of the second period, they looked a lot less dangerous.

My explanation for this is that we leaned into one of our great strengths, which is our defensive organisation and discipline. I thought Konsa was outstanding, but so too was Riccardo Calafiori at left-back whose one on one defending has improved massively. He dealt with Gakpo, he then had to contend with Rio Ngumoha, and I just loved the concentration as he focused on the ball and more often than not prevented Liverpool from creating danger.

Myles Lewis-Skelly came on midfield, Odegaard’s pressing was relentless, and as I remarked on BlueSky afterwards, if this team could attack half as well as it can defend, we’d be the best team in the world by a mile. There were moments when we could have countered better and with more pace, but we still found some threat in the second 45. The best chance fell to Tzolis, set up by Madueke, and his first-time shot was heading for the bottom corner but for a brilliant save from Alisson.

Liverpool threw the kitchen sink at it from the bench, but it made little difference. Mac Allister then got a bit naughty, slapping Odegaard on the back of the head, then collapsing to the ground to make it look as if Madueke had leaned his head into him. Replays showed that didn’t happen, and it was pretty pathetic from the Argentina international. I guess, as well as being a risible piece of play-acting, there was an element of desperation to it, because Liverpool huffed and puffed but could not blow our house down because of how defensively outstanding we are as a team.

For the first time in Premier League history, Liverpool finished a home game without a shot on target, which tells you something. It probably tells you just how much that Timber shirt pull had an impact because a striker like Isak would at least have tested David Raya from there, but more broadly it tells you that this is a team who look laser-focused on their target this season which is to retain the title – something we’ve never done in the modern era.

Afterwards, I thought the manager’s turn of phrase was interesting when he referred to it as ‘a mission’, saying:

Just loving the mission and the mission was something that we didn’t accomplish in 14 years. You really need to enjoy that. If you don’t, there will be a moment that you will switch off and they will punish you. I think the way we competed and played and the chances that we generated as well, it was really impressive so I’m really happy.

He’s obviously referencing winning away at Liverpool for the first time in such a long time, but I think it applies to the season as well. And, as I referenced in yesterday’s blog, there was a response to the midweek defeat to Fleetwood Town. If that was a result that as fans we could find relatively easy to compartmentalise, I don’t think the same is true for this manager because we know he wants to win every game, and it how much it stings when we don’t – especially against lower league opposition. He expected his side to deliver, saying:

It was a feeling, how the hell can that happen? How can you get out of the cup when you shoot 27 times? We had the chances that we had against a team that had put one shot on target and then you look so silly. Then you have to go to Anfield and say, how can I lift those players up? I had a feeling and I said, now is the moment. We’re going to have to dig deep, have an element of luck at times and for sure a lot of quality in the key moments and we’ve done it.

Which I think is a pretty fair assessment. We did a lot of stuff very well, we had moments of luck – which you so often need in a game like this to take all three points – but I don’t think anyone should be under any illusions that this was anything other than the champions demonstrating our title credentials again. In every season, regardless of how good you are, you need the rub of the green from time to time, like a Ruud van Nistelrooy penalty miss at Old Trafford, or Mateus Fernandes missing a huge chance for West Ham. It doesn’t change the inherent quality you possess or what you’re capable of doing, and in the cold light of day it should make you more driven to ensure you widen the margins – and by that I mean delivering a bit more in the opposition’s final third.

However, no complaints this morning. We had a job to do, and a difficult one at that, and we did exactly that to put us back on top of the table. It’s a nice place to be, but it’s still so early in the season I think we should dismiss any chat about what it means at this point. We can be impressed, but still cognisant of the fact there’s still a long, long way to go.

Right, I’ll leave it there for now, but we will have an Arsecast Extra for you a bit later on today. We’ve already put out the call for questions on BlueSky @gunnerblog.bsky.social and @arseblog.com, so fire away using the hashtag #arsecastextra – or if you’re an Arseblog Member on Patreon, leave your question in the #arsecast-extra-questions channel on our Discord server.

The pod should be out around around noon or so. Until then, have a good one.

#1757. Arsecast Extra Episode 719 – 02.11.2026

Welcome to another Arsecast Extra, the Arsenal podcast, with myself and James from @gunnerblog.

In this episode we look back at the massive win at Anfield on Sunday after Kai Havertz’s first half goal was enough for all three points. We analyse the Gunners strong start to the game, and opportunities to score a second, before the game swung back towards the home side in the last part of the first half. There’s discussion of Jurrien Timber’s foul on Alexander Isak which probably should have seen Liverpool awarded a penalty, and the big miss from Alexis Mac Allister, before we look at how Arsenal’s hugely impressive defensive strength kept the opposition at arm’s length for the second half, and what this result means for the title challenge even at this relatively early point of the season. In part two we answer questions about egregious play-acting, Mikel Arteta’s subs, Declan Rice’s standing in the pantheon of Arsenal signings, Bruno Guimaraes’ integration thus far, and lots more.

#1756. Fridges and pigs and scoring goals

We live in strange times. Sorry to start your day with this shocking revelation, I realise this is a bit of a bolt from the blue, but it’s fact. All across Europe supermarket fridges are being hacked. What a time to be alive. They used to hack, I dunno, mainframes and banks and shit, but now they’re hacking fridges.

Maybe they just got bored taking billions of made-up money from CryptoSloth and BitWomble and needed a challenge. I feel like fridges ought to be the kind of thing you just can’t hack – beyond unplugging it – but what do I know? Anyway, it’s an example of how the inter-connectivity that brings us all together every day is being weaponised and now the sliced meats in your local store are gone off because Neo pwned some large cold cupboards. As if we don’t have enough to deal with.

Such as all the people who hate the way Arsenal play. Let me be very clear, my days of caring what other people think about this football club, or pretty much anything else that’s important to me, are gone. It’s a waste of time. It’s a bit like quote that’s often attributed to George Bernard Shaw, which says ‘Never wrestle with pigs. You both get dirty and the pig likes it.’

I don’t think he actually said that, but I think we can all connect with the meaning. It applies so much to social media, and to many of the ways we’re exposed to punditry and ‘expert’ analysis in football these days. Like one of those shows where you have a couple of ex-pro pigs bleating on about this and that, and then a collection of other little pigs who support all the clubs argue with them and amongst themselves, and it’s just a pigstravaganza of pointless, inane bollocks but it does #numbers on socials so is seen as valuable #content.

I understand why opposition fans go on and on about how much they hate how Arsenal play. It’s because we win a lot of games. That’s the thing that really irks them. That’s just so basic though, you can’t appear to be clever and an aficionado of the game if you just say ‘I don’t like it when they win’, so it’s dressed up as dismissal of style or something else.

And look, here’s where the strange world we live in comes back into focus. You can, and really should, be able to hold more than one thought in your brain – about football or anything else – that holds true. I absolutely love how good we are defensively. LOVE IT. The commitment with which we are determined not to give the opposition anything is truly something to relish. Players laser-focused on their one on ones; putting bodies on the line to block shots and crosses; 11 players moving like a murmuration of birds because they’re so well drilled and organised; off the awareness and discipline; brilliantly timed tackles and headers and clearances; lads sticking up for each other when the opposition get a bit snide, as we saw on Sunday with Jurrien Timber and Noni Madueke refusing to allow their captain to be treated that way; it’s all part of a brilliantly defiant defensive attitude that runs right through this team.

Creating that is not easy. As Arsenal fans we have endured defences that were porous and feeble and, at times, very, very stupid. I do not long for a return to those times. Over the years Mikel Arteta has assembled a collection of players who cannot wait to go out there and do the dirty work of defending, and it runs from front to back because that’s what he demands. If it was that easy, everyone would do it, so to castigate a team’s brilliance in one department because you just lost to them without a shot on target just comes across as sour grapes.

Here’s the other thought though. I’d really like us to be a bit better from an attacking perspective, and when I look at this team and what it’s capable of, there’s no question the forward line remains the area where you can see the room for improvement. We defend as well as we do because, more often than you or I might like, we have to – because we live through games of fine margins. A 1-0 to the Arsenal is part of our history, hard-wired into our supporter DNA (particularly if you’re of a particular vintage), but I can’t lie and wish there weren’t a few more 3-0s to the Arsenal.

I’m absolutely certain Mikel Arteta would like that too, and I think it’s a bit too easy to say that this is a team that plays precisely the football he wants it to play. He is, as we all understand, an arch pragmatist, so what we get is a team that leans into its strengths, as laid out above. He is characterised as a defensive coach, which I get, but a few seasons ago we found an attacking cocktail that drove a title challenge, and saw us score more goals that year than the Invincibles did when they won the league in 2004 (91 to 73).

I think he wants both. He wants that parsimony at the back and the firepower up front. Unfortunately, forward line recruitment is the most difficult part of transfer business, and while he as manager has a part to play in that, as a club our track record is quite poor in that regard. This summer’s window was a complete bust from an attacking perspective, not a good look when you’re pursuing players like Morgan Rogers, Vinicius Junior and Julian Alvarez. When you then let three forwards go and add just one, there are questions to be asked of the people in charge. Arteta among them, of course, but he’s not the one whose job it is to get the deals done.

It’s why there are so many conversations around January, and what we might do. We see other clubs recruit forwards who produce on a consistent basis, while ours too often struggle to find that end product. Is it our system? Would these players find it hard to get those goals for us? Reasonable questions, but the bottom line in my opinion is that we have A+ options at the back and in midfield, while in that front three we’re a bit C-. That’s where the room for improvement is, that’s where the recruitment needs to be better (certainly better than no recruitment at all), and that’s how the games we currently win by a single goal margin, often by virtue of our defensive strength, become a bit more routine.

Simplistic? Yes. Easier said than done? Quite probably. But necessary? Absolutely. Until then though, expect more defensive masterclasses, more pig wrestling, and perhaps someone could hack our own Swedish fridge into scoring a few more goals. Worth a try!

Man United were stunned in September when the attacker's representatives told the English club that he wanted to leave in search of pastures new.

The teenager had been due to sign scholarship terms with the Red Devils on his 16th birthday in October, with a professional contract then expected to follow a year later.

As a result, the saga is set to come to an end in the near future.

Real Madrid allegedly want to initially use JJ Gabriel in their Castilla outfit, who operate in Spain's third division, but it is not expected to be long before the teenager secures first-team action in either La Liga or the Champions League.

JJ Gabriel made his senior debut for Man United in their pre-season game against Atletico Madrid during the summer, and he is regarded as one of the brightest young talents in world football.

The forward has a deal with Man United's academy until the end of the campaign, but the teenager has a European passport through both of his parents.

A FIFA loophole could therefore see him join Real Madrid at the start of 2027.

JJ Gabriel, who has not been at Man United's training complex since September, boasts a record of 29 goals and four assists in 32 appearances for Man United Under-18s.

#1754. Premier League star's career criminal brother beats Home Office bid to deport him to Africa - as he awaits trial for kidnap, false imprisonment, aggravated burglary and robbery

Published: 03:45 EST, 8 November 2026 | Updated: 04:38 EST, 8 November 2026

The street criminal brother of a Premier League star has beaten a Home Office attempt to deport him to Africa - by citing his own human rights.

The gang member and aspiring rapper, now in his twenties, was the subject of a concerted four year attempt by the government to send him to his family's country of origin in West Africa because of his shocking criminal record.

The young man, who has never held down a job, is currently in prison for dangerous driving and carrying a knife - while awaiting yet another court case accused of kidnap, false imprisonment, aggravated burglary and robbery.

During his teens he had played academy football for several Premier League teams but while his brother went on to make it and is now a multi-millionaire, the man instead got sucked into street crime.

And he has been involved in so much anti-social and criminal behaviour since then that he has even incurred a number of gunshot wounds.

But the wannabe rapper has managed to win a long-running deportation bid by the Home Office to kick him out of Britain as an undesirable - arguing that this wouldn't be fair as all his significant ties are here.

A Premier League footballer - who cannot be named for legal reasons - has seen his career criminal brother living in Britian beat a Home Office attempt to deport him back to West Africa

The Home Office first targeted him for deportation in 2022 after he was sentenced to 20 months in jail having been caught with a sword in his waistband, which in turn meant had breached an existing order about his criminal behaviour.

They lost that attempt to get him out of Britain but appealed - and have now lost that appeal too.

The gang member is 'healthy and capable' according to a judge but has never worked - in stark contrast to his hugely successful brother, a full international footballer who has made countless top flight appearances.

A court heard the foreign national has a 'sustained history of criminal offending involving repeated breaches of Criminal Behaviour Orders, possession of offensive weapons, breaches of licence conditions, recalls to custody, and recent charges. He has a history of offending with knives since the age of 17'.

Totaling his various jail terms together he has spent three of the last eight years prison.

But despite his ongoing recurrent criminality, the Home Office has failed in its latest attempt to deport him after a judge ruled he is 'socially and culturally integrated' into the UK and a return to his home country would leave him 'very much an outsider'.

The immigration tribunal decided he would face 'very significant obstacles to integration' in his home country and prevented the government from deporting him by ruling it would breach his human rights.

That decision came despite it emerging that he has an uncle in the country and grew up with a familiarity of the country, including its culture and food, while his mother maintains links to the country and visited as recently as 2024.

But the judge said the 'significance of these ties should not be exaggerated' because he has never been there.

They said his social and cultural identity 'has been almost entirely formed in the UK and by British culture' - even though he was born overseas and his family come from West Africa. The Home Office is appealing the decision and so the brother could still face deporation.

The knife criminal first arrived in the UK in 2006 after being born in another country where he doesn't have nationality.

He is in a relationship with a British woman with whom he shares a baby.

Their child was born in February but the rapper has only met them twice because he remains incarcerated.

There is no evidence that having a partner or child has reformed his criminal ways, a court heard.

The Home Office argued he is a healthy young adult capable of work who has a familiarity with the culture of his home country and has family ties in the country who could provide guidance and support.

But the judge concluded it would breach his human rights because he has never lived or visited and would be an outsider if returned.

#1753. Saliba returns with scope for rotation against Slavia Prague

Arsenal are in Champions League action this evening, away to Slavia Prague. There was a big boost ahead of the game with the return of William Saliba to full training, and the Frenchman is with the squad for the game this evening. Whether he starts or not is another question, but he’s clearly in good enough shape to be in contention for some minutes, and that can only be a good thing.

It was obviously a topic of conversation at the manager’s pre-game press conference yesterday evening, and provided an update on how the recovery has gone:

He’s in a really good place. I think the process and the timings and in the manner the injury has been dealt with, and especially the feelings that Willy has been having along the way, they’ve been very, very positive. So, his evolution has been as expected, which is not always the case. He feels very comfortable. He played 45 minutes behind closed doors last week and he feels ready to go. So whether we use him or not now is a matter of what the team needs.

There have rightfully been plenty of plaudits for Ezri Konsa since his arrival, and the way he’s slotted into the team, and there was a question about how he solves the two into three ‘problem’ when choosing his central defenders going forward:

So far we haven’t had that luxury, I wouldn’t call it a problem! We can talk about problems that are very different to that one. The moment that they are fit and available, we’re going to have the opportunity to give players rest or to load the players and to manage the congestion of the players in a much better way than we’ve actually done.

That is most definitely the kind of problem any manager would like to have. There’s no need to rush Saliba back, we can be cautious with his reintegration, and then when we have the problem of deciding who plays in which game, it feels very much like the kind of bridge we can cross when we come to it. But it’s a very nice bridge.

Beyond that, I think there’s some real room for rotation this evening. Players like Ben White, Cristhian Mosquera and Piero Hincapie will be looking for minutes at the back, and if we don’t see either Declan Rice or Martin Odegaard in the starting line-up this evening, I’d be absolutely fine with that. The manager can choose two World Cup winners in midfield, and still leave out one of Myles Lewis-Skelly or Bruno Guimaraes if he does that – it’s the kind of ‘luxury’ he needs to lean into.

Speaking about Mikel Merino and Martin Zubimendi, he said of their involvement so far this season:

They are playing a pivotal role. If we focus on the players that are starting, obviously that’s something else. Mikel has started some games already, some important games and he’s coming from a World Cup, a very successful World Cup. We know the value of the players that we have in the squad. They need to feel important. I do think that they feel very important and we have to make sure that they continue like that because if they have that spirit and that belief within themselves every time they play, they will make things happen for the team to win the game.

Up front, it’s a little trickier. Eberechi was a doubt for the game against Liverpool, while Christos Tzolis player almost the full 90 after his return from injury. I wonder is there any scope to start Max Dowman on the right, which means you can time-share the left between the two I just mentioned and/or Noni Madueke. I think you also have to look at this as another chance for Viktor Gyokeres who did get on the scoresheet against Fleetwood, but on a night when any kind of confidence boost that might have provided was offset by the fact we lost to lower league opposition. His minutes have been a bit scarce so far this season, but you’d be very hard pressed to argue that when he has played he’s done enough to give the manager much to think about. He could really use goals and a decent performance this evening.

I suppose that defeat to Fleetwood might give Arteta some pause for thought when it comes to how much he might rotate, but if you can’t give players minutes in games like this, then they’re not going to be in the kind of shape you need them be in if and when they’re required for more challenging fixtures. It’s not to take anything for granted against a side who are top of their domestic league, but in Europe this season they’ve been a bit poor, and if this isn’t the time to test our squad depth, I don’t know what is. Let’s see!

Before we go today, Andrew Allen has a feature in his weekly Patreon newsletter which covers match day recommendations. It started with restaurants/bars etc close to the ground, but has expanded over time into something much more global. With the help of @bootifulgame.bsky.social – they’ve built a really cool interactive tool which you can check out here – https://matchday.arseblog.com/ – and which now exists as a permanent feature on this site.

We often get questions about ‘Where can I watch with Arsenal fans when I’m in X city’ etc, and there are already lots of places listed around the world. If you want to add to the map, you can submit a recommendation to show where your local bar or venue is, and if you’re travelling somewhere, this is the perfect reference for when there’s an Arsenal game on and you want to hang out with fellow fans. It’s real community project, designed to bring supporters together, and which can improve over time with your help.

I’m sure it’s going to be really useful, and we’ll try and build it into the apps going forward too.

Right, I’ll leave it there for this morning. As ever, we’ll bring you live blog coverage of the game later, as well all the post-game stuff on Arseblog News like the match report, player ratings, manager reaction, quotes round-up and more. Don’t forget the updated Arseblog apps also have a cool new matchday centre, full of stats, alerts, and much more.

#1752. Tactics Column: High alert at the back stick

A long overdue win at Anfield was marked by a goal, a number of other Arsenal chances, and what will go down as a famous clean sheet, all involving how the two teams defend at the back post.

There were plenty of other interesting things to note on Sunday – Martin Odegaard’s role drifting across the pitch early on and Arsenal’s 20-odd minute spell of dominance midway through the second half both caught the eye – but in the latest instalment of our video series Between The Lines, I look into how Arsenal had great joy attacking the back post, and why Liverpool were never going to have the same luck at the other end.

With the hosts’ defence getting narrow in their own box, Arsenal created plenty of opportunities by having the man on the far side outside that defensive block. That’s how Kai Havertz scored, it’s how he nearly tapped in from Bruno Guimaraes’ effort that flew just wide, and it’s how Noni Madueke nearly teed Havertz up with another tap-in. It’s also where Christos Tzolis was positioned as he came onto a Madueke cross and forced Alisson into the game’s standout save.

Arsenal, though, have no such weakness: their combination of organisation, hunger, and (perhaps most importantly) focus meant Liverpool were never likely to find a spare man at the back post.

#1751. Dowman weaves his magic and new signing shines as Arsenal hit ground running

Teenage sensation Max Dowman was the star of Arsenal’s first pre-season match, as he scored one goal and assisted another in a 4-1 victory over Girona.

Dowman, 16, was joined on the scoresheet by new signing Christos Tzolis, who struck with a low effort in his first game since his £34m move from Belgian side Club Brugge.

Established attackers Kai Havertz and Gabriel Jesus also scored for the Premier League champions, who were largely comfortable against opposition from the Spanish second tier.

Here are four things Telegraph Sport learnt from the match:

It was this time last year that Dowman first announced his remarkable talent to the wider world. Then only 15, he sparkled in pre-season and made it clear to Mikel Arteta that he was ready to impact matches at the highest level.

A year on, Dowman is now an established first-team player. He is the youngest ever Premier League winner and the competition’s youngest ever scorer, and he looks set to make even more of a mark this season.

In this friendly against Girona, Dowman created Arsenal’s opening goal with a gorgeous defence-splitting pass for Havertz. He did so after receiving the ball under pressure and spinning into space. Dowman then scored Arsenal’s third with a powerful low drive from the edge of the box.

Dowman is in competition with Bukayo Saka and Noni Madueke for a place on the right wing, which means this summer represents a huge opportunity for the teenager. After playing for England at the World Cup, Saka and Madueke will both miss most of pre-season.

Dowman, therefore, has a serious chance of going into the new campaign as the starting right-winger. The Community Shield on August 16 must be a target in his mind.

“We know what he’s capable of doing,” Arteta said. “We want to be more consistent in terms of the performances and the actions that he can deliver, but I think today he had a really good game.”

Arsenal are close to completing a deal for Newcastle United captain Bruno Guimarães but, for now, their only outfield signing of the summer has been Tzolis. This was the Greek winger’s first match in front of supporters and he immediately demonstrated why Arsenal were willing to pay £34m to buy him from Club Brugge.

With Tzolis, it is all about the final product. Goals and assists. He struck 22 times for Club Brugge last season, and registered 29 assists.

How did he produce such impressive numbers? The answer could be seen in his first-half goal against Girona. Receiving the ball on the left wing, Tzolis quickly accelerated towards the penalty area and unleashed a low shot. It was perhaps a more direct approach than Arsenal would usually have seen from Leandro Trossard, the player Tzolis has replaced, and it caught Girona off-guard as the ball deflected into the net.

“I’m very pleased with him,” Arteta said. “First of all, the way he has adapted to the club, to the team. The connection he’s already generating with the boys. I think you’re going to love the player.

“A player who’s very direct. He’s got the goal between the eyes. He has a lot of similarities with Leo [Trossard] in a lot of the things that he can do and the spaces he can occupy. And then the work rate that he has... He’s a boy that comes with so much hunger. He wants to prove himself, it’s a dream for him. And we are here to help him.”

Havertz was one of the few Arsenal players who benefited from playing at the World Cup. His injury issues mean that, unlike most of his team-mates, he did not end the 2025-26 season in a state of exhaustion.

After returning to the pitch in the spring, Havertz enjoyed an impressive end to the campaign for Arsenal. He then performed well at the World Cup, scoring three goals for Germany.

He remains one of Arteta’s favourite players, not least because of his versatility. He started in attack in the crucial end-of-season games in May, but played in midfield against Girona. His low finish, from Dowman’s pass, represented his eighth goal in his last 12 matches for club and country.

Girona’s goal, scored by Arnau Martínez, was perhaps the only alarming moment of this comfortable pre-season victory. Martínez was unmarked from a left-wing corner when he powered a header into Arsenal’s net.

For a group of players who pride themselves on their set-piece prowess, this was a disappointing moment. It also perhaps showed Arsenal’s reliance on their two first-choice centre-backs, William Saliba and Gabriel Magalhães, when they are defending crosses into their box.

Gabriel arrived at Arsenal’s pre-season training camp a few days ago, so he should be in good shape by the start of the new campaign. Saliba, though, will be missing for months with a back problem.

Without Saliba’s height and power, will Arsenal be as effective from set-pieces in the opening chunk of the campaign? Coventry City, Arsenal’s opponents on the first night of the season, will undoubtedly look to test the champions in these situations.

The reigning Premier League champions are handed the Costa Brava Trophy, which is half-heartedly lifted into the air by White. There will be far bigger trophies on offer to Arsenal in the upcoming campaign.

Arsenal have cruised to a routine 4-1 win over Girona, with Havertz, Tzolis, Dowman and Gabriel Jesus all finding the net. Arteta will be delighted with his side’s professionalism and ruthlessness.

Meslier takes too long on his goal kick, gifting a corner to Girona. However, the delivery from the hosts is so poor as it flies harmlessly out of play. That sums up Girona’s difficult evening.

There is another round of substitutions for both sides.

Two more changes in the offing...↩️ Jesus, Copley🔛 Agustien, Julienne🔴 1-4 🔵 (85) pic.twitter.com/3qt6N63qzq

🔁 Últim canvi al Girona:➡️ Stuani⬅️ Pyshchur

Once again, Meslier makes a pivotal stop on his Arsenal debut. Martin clips an exquisite pass over Arsenal’s defence to the onrushing Ruiz, who is through on goal. The striker takes the chance first time, but Meslier is there to make another crucial save.

Arsenal’s makeshift line-up, which is full of Hale End graduates, is holding firm, with Girona evidently struggling for attacking inspiration. If Arsenal can see out this victory without any injuries, then it would have panned out exactly how Arteta would have wanted.

Girona carelessly give possession away in defence, allowing Nelson to dribble towards the penalty area. The winger floats a cross into the box, which is met by O’Neill, but the forward’s lofted header hits the top of the bar.

There is cooling break in this second half to give both sets of players a quick breather. It’s been a professional performance from Arsenal, who now have various academy prospects on the pitch. Can any of them follow in Dowman’s footsteps and make an eye-catching impression in this match?

Girona make another flurry of changes, giving the youngsters from the club’s academy an opportunity to impress.

🔁 Més canvis al Girona:➡️ Gibert, Holmes, Izan, Misehouy i Jastin⬅️ Arnau, Fran Beltrán, Francés, Bryan i Minsu pic.twitter.com/fb7aVKloFx

Kabia gets to the byline and intelligently pulls a cross back to Gabriel Jesus, who curls a first-time strike narrowly wide of the far post as Arsenal search for a fifth goal.

Dowman was the breakout star of pre-season last year, when he was only 15, and he has started this campaign in similarly thrilling fashion. One assist, one goal. As you would expect, he looks bigger and stronger.

Arsenal overturn the ball in midfield and it breaks perfectly into the Brazilian’s path. Gabriel Jesus is one-on-one and makes no mistake, applying a devastating finish to make it 4-1 and put the result beyond any doubt.

The 16-year-old prodigy now has a goal and an assist. Dowman picks up the ball in the right attacking pocket, palms off Moreno, who bizarrely throws himself to the ground holding his face, before firing a resounding effort into the bottom corner. He’s such a talented footballer and looks at home in Arsenal’s first team.

Out of nothing, Girona have pulled a goal back. Kim whips a corner into the box, with the unmarked Martinez slamming a magnificent header into the top corner, leaving Kepa rooted to the spot. Arteta will be furious with his side’s complacency there.

🎯 El gol d'Arnau pic.twitter.com/Op6oX3LBzK

The team known as “Set Piece FC” looked alarmingly vulnerable at that Girona corner. Perhaps this is simply the reality of life without William Saliba and Gabriel Magalhaes. The good news for Arsenal is that Gabriel is back with the squad and should be ready to go for the start of the campaign. The bad news is that Saliba’s back injury will rule him out for months. Will that lead to more sustained vulnerability over the opening chunk of the season?

Girona have sent a host of players out to warm up. They’re playing in their fourth pre-season match, with their league campaign due to start on August 16 against Leganes.

We are back under way for the second half.

That was a straightforward half for Arsenal. Arteta will be pleased with Havertz’s showing in his 33 minutes on the pitch. After missing so much of last season through injury, it has been a good summer for Havertz so far. He scored three goals in Arsenal’s final six games of 2025/26, and then netted four times for Germany in June.

The 2009-born playmaker was Arsenal’s standout player in that first half. Dowman’s confidence and class on the ball has been brilliant, with his expertly-crafted assist for Havertz’s opener an obvious highlight.

Arsenal are in complete control here in Spain thanks to first-half strikes from Havertz and Tzolis.

A dominant first-half display in Girona 🙌 pic.twitter.com/ZprG2xLYyj

Dowman dribbles into the penalty area with ease, drifting past a couple of defenders before he is apprehended by Moreno. He goes down, but there is very little in the challenge.

Arsenal are in cruise control here. Girona are chasing shadows. Unsurprisingly, there’s a real gulf in class and quality between the two sides.

Once again, Dowman dances away from Moreno. The youngster sets up White with a reverse pass, but the Arsenal captain’s disappointing cross drifts out for a goal kick.

Tzolis registered 22 goals and 29 assists for Club Brugge last season. He is an end-product machine, and that goal was a little indication of how he racks up such eye-watering numbers. After receiving possession on the left wing, he was so quick to shift the ball onto his right foot and fire the shot at goal. He describes himself as a “direct” player and that was evidence of it.

There are three early changes for Arsenal, with Gyokeres, Havertz and Hincapie taken off for Gabriel Jesus, Vieira and Salmon.

We're making a triple substitution...↩️ Havertz, Hincapie, Gyokeres🔛 Vieira, Salmon, Jesus🔴 0-2 🔵 (32) pic.twitter.com/NtpnUsfAY6

The new winger is one-on-one with Martinez and darts inside, before firing a low effort into the bottom corner. It took a slight deflection, leaving Gazzaniga with no chance. Tzolis has looked lively and slotted into Arsenal’s attack seamlessly so far.

Tzolis is slipped into the penalty area from his left-wing berth, but instead of shooting, he tries to find Gyokeres with a pass. Girona surround the Swede before Dowman’s follow-up strike is blocked.

Since their goal, Arsenal have assumed real authority of this encounter and look like the far superior side.

Girona captain Martinez slams a powerful long-range effort at goal, but it fizzes wide of the bottom corner. Kepa seemed to have it covered regardless.

Arsenal are hunting for a second, with Lewis-Skelly picking out Havertz with a floated pass. The former Chelsea man is inches away from teeing up Gyokeres for a second, but Gazzaniga is there to make a goal-saving interception. Dowman has also been heavily involved in these early stages, providing the assist for Havertz’s opener.

After his extraordinary breakthrough campaign last year, Max Dowman has a huge opportunity this summer. With England wingers Bukayo Saka and Noni Madueke not returning until later in pre-season, Dowman has a chance to take ownership of the right wing position ahead of the Community Shield. His assist for Kai Havertz, a lovely measured pass after an excellent piece of skill in midfield, was a sign that Dowman means business.

Dowman drifts inside and pops up in the right channel, wriggling past Moreno, before threading a delightful pass through to Havertz. One-on-one, the German calmly slots a close-range effort into the bottom corner, giving Arsenal a well-deserved lead. So much credit must go to Dowman, who has started this game excellently.

Girona have some sustained possession to take the sting out of the game then burst into Arsenal’s penalty area, with the ball attempted to be pulled back to Van De Beek. The visitors have good numbers defending and comfortably deal with the danger.

Tzolis floats a free kick into the box, which Gyokeres meets at the back post. The striker directs the ball back across goal towards Calafiori, whose close-range header is caught by Gazzaniga.

It also appears that Havertz and Nwaneri have been tasked with quite free-roaming attacking midfield roles, with Lewis-Skelly positioned as a one-man holding pivot. It’s a strong but experimental line-up from Arteta.

After suffering an injury at the end of last season and missing the World Cup, White returns to action here this evening and wears the armband. He will look to support Dowman, who appears to be starting on the right wing.

It’s been a confident start from Arsenal, who are stroking the ball around in a very assured manner. Havertz looks to pull the strings by firing a low cross towards Gyokeres, but the delivery is scrambled clear by the Girona backline.

White leads Arsenal out onto the pitch to face Girona, who boast the likes of Van de Beek, Gil and Moreno in their starting XI.

Talking earlier this week, Arsenal boss Mikel Arteta sent out a determined message to other clubs by outlining their ambitious transfer plans.

“A lot is happening,” Arteta said. “We all know about the context of this transfer window. From ownership to the board, the sporting director and myself, we know that we want to take this club to a different level.

“That is going to require a better squad, better individuals. We have identified where we have opportunities to grow and to improve and to evolve our game and what is going to be needed to achieve that. Hopefully very soon we can start to put things in a very concrete way.”

Arteta also believes that last season’s Premier League title has served as added motivation for his squad to improve and hit new heights.

“This has to be the start and this has to be the standard,” he said. “Excellence has to be our standard and this has to drive to attack the future. The way we behave daily with more and more determination and ambition, because we’ve shown that we’ve got it. Now we have to show that we belong to this level and we want to increase and take this football club to a different dimension.”

It had been a relatively quiet transfer window for Arsenal, who have recruited just goalkeeper Illan Meslier and winger Christos Tzolis.

However, Arsenal are now moving very bullishly, closing on Newcastle United midfielder Bruno Guimarães, while also targeting Real Madrid’s Vinícius Júnior.

Sam Dean has the full breakdown of a potential deal for the Real Madrid star and how Arsenal are prepared to continue flexing their muscles in the transfer market in what would be one of the biggest moves in Premier League history.

It was January 2025, with Arsenal earning a hard-fought 2-1 comeback victory in the Champions League courtesy of first-half goals from Jorginho and Ethan Nwaneri.

Since this European encounter, Girona have been on a seriously downward trajectory, enduring lowly 16th and 19th finishes in La Liga, with the latter ensuring relegation to the Segunda Division, where they’ll play in the upcoming campaign.

August 5: Arsenal vs Real Betis (Dublin, Ireland)

August 9: Arsenal vs Borussia Dortmund (London, England)

August 12: Arsenal vs Como (London, England)

August 16: Arsenal vs Manchester City (Cardiff, Wales)

Mikel Arteta’s side will then begin their defence of the Premier League title on August 21 when they host newly-promoted Coventry City on August 21.

Arsenal are closing in on one of the statement signings of the summer, with Newcastle United midfielder Bruno Guimarães getting closer to joining the Premier League holders.

This deal means that Christian Norgaard is expected to leave and seal a move to Everton for around £7m.

As previously reported by Telegraph Sport, Guimarães has been Arsenal’s top target for weeks. It is believed that he will cost around £80m.

#1750. Netherlands vs Greece - prediction, team news, lineups

By Jonathan O'Shea | 11 Nov 2026 16:28, Last updated: 11 Nov 2026 19:37

Potentially deciding who takes top spot in Group 2, the Netherlands and Greece will meet in Amsterdam for a UEFA Nations League clash on Friday evening.

Both unbeaten after four games - and level on eight points apiece - the sides are set to convene for their penultimate League A fixture.

With two rounds remaining, the fight for a qualification from Group 2 remains close, with the Netherlands and Greece only separated by goals scored - in that respect, the Greeks trail by two.

Meanwhile, traditional heavyweights Germany sit just three points behind in third place, and only the top two will go through to the Nations League quarter-finals.

So far, the Netherlands have won twice and twice fought back to draw, showing plenty of character under new national coach Xavi.

Cody Gakpo's late strike stole a point against old foes Germany on matchday one, before home and away wins over rock-bottom Serbia were split by a thrilling game in Greece.

Trailing 2-0 as the final half-hour approached, Oranje roared back to claim a draw, thanks to goals from captain Virgil van Dijk and impact substitute Tijjani Reijnders.

All of which means three points from Friday's reverse fixture could see them potentially confirm entry to the knockout phase, which will begin early next year.

That 2-2 draw in Thessaloniki was as close as Greece have come to beating their Dutch counterparts in a senior competitive match.

Extending a long reign of dominance, the Netherlands had previously won both qualifiers between the pair en route to Euro 2024, but the Greeks will be buoyed by their meeting on matchday three.

Only promoted from League B last time around, the Galanolefki are still undefeated at Europe's elite level, as a talented new generation breaks through.

After overturning a deficit to beat Serbia in their opener - via a stoppage-time winner from Como striker Tasos Douvikas - they followed up with an impressive 1-0 win over Germany.

Having subsequently come within minutes of upsetting the Netherlands, three days later they held Jurgen Klopp and co to a goalless home draw.

Firmly in contention for a quarter-final berth, Ivan Jovanovic's side will now aim to build on that momentum with an historic success at Johan Cruijff Arena.

The hosts must negotiate their final pair of group games without Ryan Gravenberch, Kenneth Taylor, Brian Brobbey and Van Dijk, all of whom have withdrawn due to injury.

Brentford's Sepp van den Berg has been drafted in as cover for Oranje's vastly experienced skipper, who received his 100th international cap last month.

Juventus midfielder Teun Koopmeiners partnered Van Dijk against Serbia, but the more conventional North London duo of Jan Paul van Hecke and Jurrien Timber are likely to play on Friday night.

Mexx Meerdink impressed in Xavi's first camp, yet Donyell Malen will expect to start after returning to the squad, having scored 14 goals in 12 Roma appearances this season.

Another Serie A star, Douvikas recently netted a Champions League hat-trick; however, he faces a fight to displace Vangelis Pavlidis or Fotis Ioannidis in the visitors' front line.

In fact, Jovanovic has plenty of attacking options to choose from, including Konstantinos Karetsas and Premier League pair Christos Tzolis and Charalampos Kostoulas.

After picking up their second booking of the campaign against Germany, both Christos Zafeiris and Manolis Saliakas must serve a one-match ban; the latter's absence offers a chance for Lazaros Rota or Georgios Vagiannidis to start at right-back.

Verbruggen; Dumfries, J. Timber, Van Hecke, Van de Ven; Q. Timber, De Jong, Veerman; Summerville, Malen, Gakpo

Tzolakis; Vagiannidis, Mavropanos, Koulierakis, Tsimikas; Masouras, Kourbelis, Androutsos, Tzolis; Ionannidis, Pavlidis

As the Netherlands can be caught out at the back - and their visitors have a bright crop of attacking talent - there should be more goals, after the teams' entertaining contest last month.

Though Greece are a rising force, their unbeaten streak could come to an end, as Xavi can welcome back Malen and Frenkie de Jong - even if his injured captain will be missed.

#1747. Slavia Prague 1-2 Arsenal: Slight concerns but another away day win

Arsenal secured another away win last night, this time in the Champions League beating Slavia Prague 2-1 thanks to goals from Noni Madueke and Viktor Gyokeres.

Mikel Arteta rotated in some areas, with starts for Ben White, Piero Hincapie, Martin Zubimendi, Mikel Merino and Eberechi Eze, but relied too on the foundational stability of Declan Rice with Ezri Konsa and Gabriel behind him. We began in lively fashion, and took an early lead.

David Raya played it long, Gyokeres held it up well and hooked the ball forward, and Madueke’s pace took him beyond the defender and into the box before finishing between the keeper’s legs. Solid play from two players who can sometimes be guilty of fluffing their lines when it comes to those key actions. This time they were spot on.

We had more chances to score. Eze showed nice skills in the box but saw his shot blocked; Gyokeres headed back across goal for Merino but he headed over; the Spaniard saw a shot from distance tipped over, and his smart near post run and a right-footed shot from a Ben White cutback forced the keeper into another decent stop; and there was a brilliant counter and pass from Rice that drifted all the way to the back post without any Arsenal player attacking it for a tap-in.

We did find a second though. Gyokeres combined well with Merino around their box, and when he was played through he opened up his body really well and produced a fine finish from close range and a tight angle to make it 2-0. I don’t think that goal at Fleetwood would have done much for his confidence, this felt much more like the kind of strike he needed to produce – for himself as much as the team.

So, we had a good lead at the break, but this was very much a game of two halves. In the first we had 60% possession, out-shot the opposition by 8 to 2, and passed at nearly 90% success rate. In the second, the tables turned. Slavia Prague took 17 shots to our 4, and our pass success fell to 77%. We were sloppy and untidy, they made a tactical change at half-time which worked well for them, and while we weren’t necessarily under the cosh, the entire dynamic of the game changed and we couldn’t get to grips with it.

We needed David Raya to make one superb save to keep them at bay, before Gabriel had to head one off the line, but in injury time they found the goal I think their second half performance (and ours) probably merited. They whipped in a wicked ball from the left, the striker applied the close range finish, and the clean sheet was gone.

Afterwards, Mikel Arteta was happy with the win, but displeased with the second half, saying:

First of all, you have to value the fact it’s very difficult to win away from home. We’ve done it against a very tough opponent, we expected that toughness. In the first half we played at a really high level in terms of intensity, tempo, quality and clarity in what we had to do, and what the game was demanding. We were very efficient – we should have scored three, four or five.

I already talked about some of the things we didn’t do, and others I’d prefer not to mention. It’s a huge lesson, and we’ll learn from the second half. It’s our third away game in quick succession, and we’re the only team to have played three away games in the Champions League and just one at home – there are a lot of factors – but I don’t like to use that, because in the first half we were at the level we wanted. I take full responsibility for the drop in the second half.

I don’t think the team played well at all in the second half, but I do wonder about how we might have done things differently. For example, I feel like Declan Rice played within himself in that second period, and let me be clear, I understand why. Personally, I think it’s a bit mad he did 90+ minutes in a game like this, even if I accept he and the manager know more about his fitness than any of us. Maybe they need him to be like a steam train, going going going all the time, but when you have options of the quality of Myles Lewis-Skelly and Bruno Guimaraes on the bench, surely using them in his stead allows the best of two worlds: some rest for Rice, and fresher legs in midfield when the game is tilting in the opposition’s favour.

We have this really strong bench, but I don’t think the changes we made worked particularly well. The question, of course, is if they absolutely needed to. We had a two goal lead until late on, and we secured all three points away from home after a difficult and physically demanding game at Anfield three days previously. I just found the Jekyll and Hyde nature of of the two halves a little concerning, but only a little. Ten of our sixteen games this season have been away from home, we’ve won seven of them, so that’s a decent return, added to by this victory.

Ultimately, this is essentially a forgettable Champions League tie that we came away with three points from. Apparently it was a year to the day since we played Slavia Prague last season too, a game I had/have zero recollection of. Which might say something about me more than anything else, but these kinds of fixtures don’t live long in the memory. They’re grist for the mill in this part of the season, we had a job to do, and we got it done, and now all the focus turns to Hull on Saturday and the three points required there before the Interlull.

We can talk a bit more about this game in an Arsecast a bit later on this morning, before I head to London a bit later on this afternoon. For those who have registered to come to the launch of The 22 tomorrow at Big Red, please remember you can purchase the book via the email sent to you (check your junk folders if you don’t see it), so you can simply come and collect on the night. We can also facilitate sales via credit card etc if you don’t want to do that.

If you purchased via the Patreon pre-sale, those books are not for collection tomorrow, and will be shipped to you in due course. There is also some scope to come along on spec on the night, and we should have copies available but obviously priority goes to those who registered. We will then have a final batch of books going on general sale online on Saturday evening after the Hull game. Full details of that to follow here on site and via Arseblog on BlueSky.

Ok, I’ll leave it there for now. Pod will be out mid-morning, until then, have a good one.

#1745. Next Man United manager: Thoughts of Red Devils dressing room on potential Unai Emery arrival 'revealed'

By Matt Law | 11 Nov 2026 16:46, Last updated: 11 Nov 2026 16:49

A number of Manchester United players had allegedly been hoping that the club would appoint Unai Emery as their next head coach.

Michael Carrick is expected to be sacked by the 20-time English champions, with an announcement from the club potentially coming on Thursday.

Mauricio Pochettino, who is in charge of the United States, is set to be appointed as the club's new head coach once Carrick's exit has been confirmed.

However, according to talkSPORT, a number of Man United players had been hoping that the club would bring in Emery as their next manager.

Emery is admired by senior figures at Man United, but the Spaniard is in discussions with Aston Villa over a new long-term contract.

The 55-year-old's existing deal is due to run until June 2029, but an announcement over an extension is expected in the not too distant future.

Earlier this month, Emery revealed that discussions were taking place over keeping him at Villa Park on an even longer basis.

"My ambition is to keep our consistency and how we are improving and building lots of things positively. It is a huge challenge," the Villa boss told reporters.

"They decided, speaking with us last year, to build a new stand to add more supporters at Villa Park. That is a clear step forward to get better.

"How we are increasing our budget each year, and revenue through our performance by playing in Europe and improving players, selling players, then buying young talented players, this is the process and ambition we should keep in the future.

"I had a good meeting with Nassef Sawiris, very good meeting, very positive. Let's talk next week, trying to get everything we spoke about together. We were speaking about how we can set our project stronger with a deal, yes."

Man United faced Villa in the Premier League last time out, twice coming from two goals behind to draw 4-4 with Emery's side at Old Trafford.

The Red Devils will return to action against Liverpool at Anfield on November 22, and the expectation is that Pochettino will be in charge for that contest.

#1744. Careless Liverpool concede same goal twice in second-half capitulation against Leeds

Leeds United came from 2-0 down at half-time to beat Liverpool 4-2 at Soldier Field in Chicago as Andoni Iraola’s side were undone by sloppy defending in the second period.

Liverpool’s dominant first-half display was underlined by goals from Luke Chambers and Florian Wirtz. However, Daniel Farke’s men replied with four strikes in 25 second-half minutes through Sean Longstaff, Brenden Aaronson and two alarmingly similar goals from Dominic Calvert-Lewin.

🎯 "CALVERT-LEWIN ARRIVES!" pic.twitter.com/CaHOeXQn7E

🤩 "Calvert-Lewin makes it FOUR!" pic.twitter.com/mEEi882OWi

Liverpool centre-back Chambers, 22, who spent last season on loan at Charlton Athletic, opened the scoring on seven minutes, pouncing on a Dominik Szoboszlai corner which had been flicked on at the near post by Milos Kerkez.

Jeremie Frimpong, serviced by a wonderfully flighted cross-field ball by Trey Nyoni, then set up Wirtz to make it 2-0 five minutes before the break, but on the hour Leeds began their recovery when Aaronson scored following a mistake by Kerkez – who gave up possession to Ethan Ampadu in his own half.

GOAL! Aaronson pulls one back! 2-1 pic.twitter.com/tdy17cITSd

Ampadu’s long throw was flicked on to Calvert-Lewin to level the score, then minutes later Curtis Jones’s carelessness allowed Longstaff in to put Leeds in front.

🔥 "LONGSTAFF! WHAT A TURNAROUND!" pic.twitter.com/G9LvLIk0Mi

And it was a familiar story five minutes from time when Ampadu’s throw again prompted chaos in Liverpool’s back line, allowing Calvert-Lewin to steal in front of Jones and seal victory.

Liverpool return to Anfield for friendlies against Monaco and Como before they begin their Premier League season away at Newcastle United later this month.

Leeds have matches against RB Leipzig, Manchester United and Augsburg before their league campaign gets under way at Nottingham Forest.
